slides: Okay, a quick summary before the advanced practice.
The ideas from the last examples... in about three minutes.
"Not necessarily true" questions. Check every statement against the definitions.
Not sure? Sketch an extreme version of the shape, very wide and very low, and just look.
A diagonal splits a parallelogram, and that includes a rectangle, a rhombus, a square, into two equal halves.
Now, a triangle on the full base, with its tip on the opposite side, is half the shape. So the white parts are the other half.
And if it's on a third of the base? Then it's a third of a half... one sixth.
Two triangles with the same height? The area ratio is the base ratio.
Say a trapezoid with bases three and twelve is cut by a diagonal. The top triangle is seven, so the bottom one is four times as much, twenty-eight. Together, that's thirty-five.
Shaded area? Approach one: take a shape you know, and subtract the white. Like sixty minus twenty-four... thirty-six.
Approach two: break the shaded area into familiar pieces, by completions or by symmetry.
Now, with completions, pair only pieces that really complete each other. A guess by eye is not a method.
Angles with letters in the answers? Solve it, or plug in numbers and check every choice.
Congruent rectangles? Read the hidden ratio off the figure. Then one unknown, x, is enough.
And you can check from the answers. Plug one back into the figure, and test the number you were given.
When you cut a shape into pieces, the cut belongs to both pieces. So it counts twice.
A staircase has the perimeter of its rectangle. So nine wide and six tall gives thirty.
But a notch is different. Its two walls are extra, so add two times its depth.
A rectangle, and you're given the perimeter and the diagonal? Well, you don't need the sides.

The perimeter is twenty-eight, so a plus b is fourteen. The diagonal is ten, so a squared plus b squared is a hundred. Now, a hundred and ninety-six is a hundred plus two a b... so the area is forty-eight.
Or try a triple. Six, eight, ten. The perimeter is twenty-eight, so it fits.
Okay, before you practice, ask yourself these questions.
And the traps: pairing pieces by eye, taking "same area" to mean "congruent", and giving an area answer to a perimeter question.
Good luck.
